analysis.one_liner: Charges a rising fee on fossil fuels and returns the money to Americans as monthly dividends.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in three House committees until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with no hearing or vote, despite bipartisan sponsorship by three Republicans and six Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge oil refineries, coal mines, natural gas pipeline operators, and importers a fee based on the greenhouse gases their fuels produce — starting at $15 per ton and rising $10 each year. Nearly all of that money would be returned as an equal monthly dividend to every U.S. citizen and lawful resident, one share per adult and half a share per child. It would also tax fluorinated greenhouse gases, add border fees on carbon-intensive imports, and suspend certain EPA carbon rules as long as the fee is working. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen and lawful resident would receive a monthly dividend paid from the carbon fees, with the bill directing that the dividend not count against eligibility for other federal benefits. Because each adult gets an equal share while higher earners consume more energy, lower- and middle-income households would typically receive more than the price increases cost them. Farmers would be exempted from fuel fees, and facilities that capture and store carbon dioxide would get refunds. Clean energy businesses would gain as fossil fuels became steadily more expensive.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a carbon fee on producers and importers of oil, natural gas, and coal, starting at $15 per ton in 2019 and increasing $10 each year, with larger increases if emissions targets are missed.

Deposits the fees into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund and pays an equal monthly dividend to every eligible adult, half a share for each child under 19, with the dividend not counted as income or resources for federal benefit programs.
Requires fee refunds for farms' fuel use and for facilities that capture and permanently store carbon dioxide.
Adds border fees on carbon-intensive imports like steel, aluminum, and cement and refunds on exports, so U.S. manufacturers are not undercut by producers in countries without carbon pricing.
Sets an emissions schedule aiming for deep reductions from 2015 levels by 2050, and speeds up the fee if emissions targets are missed.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refineries, coal mining operations, natural gas pipeline operators, and fuel importers would pay the fee directly, and much of it would reach consumers as higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. Heavy users of energy — large homes, long commutes, energy-intensive businesses — would pay more than they receive in dividends.

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel costs would rise every year, and while the equal per-person dividend exceeds the added costs for most lower- and middle-income households, high-energy-use households and some businesses would pay more than they receive.

As long as the fee is in force, the bill suspends EPA rules that limit greenhouse gas emissions from fuels, trading existing regulation for the price signal — the suspension expires if the emissions targets are not met, but critics of this approach argue that swapping regulation for a fee that a future Congress could repeal is a real risk.
Dividend payments are counted as taxable income, slightly reducing their value for recipients who owe federal tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is built to be progressive: an equal per-person dividend means most Americans, especially those with lower incomes, would come out ahead even after paying higher energy prices, while the largest payments come from the heaviest fossil fuel users. The main honest tradeoffs are the price shock during the transition years and the swap of EPA carbon rules for a fee — though the bill includes a safety valve that revives regulation if emissions targets are missed. It is a more redistribution-friendly approach than most carbon tax proposals.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced five weeks before the session ended and referred to three committees, none of which ever took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 27, 2018, by Rep. Theodore Deutch with Republicans Brian Fitzpatrick and Francis Rooney and Democrats John Delaney and Charlie Charl...
It was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs, with no subsequent committee action listed in the record.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The nine cosponsors split three Republicans and six Democrats, an unusual bipartisan lineup for climate legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal producers and utilities benefited from the bill's death, since it would have charged them a fee rising $10 per ton every year. Nothing else changed: no dividends were paid, no fossil fuel producers paid fees, and existing EPA authority remained untouched.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines: of the nine cosponsors, three were Republicans and six were Democrats, including two Republicans who helped introduce the bill — rare for climate legislation, though no vote was ever held to measure it.

industries.note: Refineries, coal mines, natural gas pipeline operators, and fuel importers would pay the carbon fee directly, with the cost rising $10 per ton annually. In this bill their added cost funds the public dividend, so their interest runs against the public's gain.

industries.industry: Clean energy and renewable energy companies
industries.note: A steadily rising fossil fuel fee would make solar, wind, and efficiency technologies more competitive each year. Their growth would come from the same price signal that funds household dividends.

industries.industry: Steel, aluminum, cement, glass, and chemical manufacturers
industries.note: These energy-intensive industries would pay more for fuel, but the border adjustment would charge similar fees on competing imports and refund fees on exports, shielding them from foreign producers without carbon pricing.

Facilities that capture and permanently store carbon dioxide would receive refunds of the carbon fee, creating a direct revenue stream for capture technology. The climate benefit depends on the storage being permanent, which the bill leaves to regulation.
Farm fuel purchases would be exempted from the carbon fee, and on-farm non-fossil emissions would not be charged, sparing farmers the cost increase other fuel buyers would face.
